organizations/formosan-presbyterian-chur.content:
Formosan Presbyterian Church in Los Angeles (FPCLA)
Formosan Presbyterian Church in Los Angeles (FPCLA) was the first Taiwanese Presbyterian church established in North America, founded in 1970 in Los Angeles, California. The church was established under the United Presbyterian Church in the USA (UPCUSA, now PC(USA)) system and served as a spiritual anchor for Taiwanese immigrants in Southern California.
Identity Snapshot

Chinese name: 洛杉磯台美人基督教會 (literal); 福爾摩沙長老教會 (Formosan Presbyterian Church)
Founded: 1970
Location: Los Angeles, California
Denomination: United Presbyterian Church in the USA (UPCUSA/PC(USA))
Type: Taiwanese-language Presbyterian congregation
Status: Historical founding church; FPCLA lineage continued through subsequent Taiwanese Presbyterian churches

Founding History
Predecessor: Taiyou Church (太陽教會)
Before FPCLA, an experimental church called “Taiyou Church” (太陽教會, “Sun Church”) was associated with Rev. Jonah Chang (張瑞雄) (c. 1967 Japanese Methodist facility context; B-tier). This experiment laid the groundwork for a separate Taiwanese congregation.
Founding Process (1970)
FPCLA was founded through the collaboration of:

Taiwanese believers: A group of Taiwanese immigrants including Dr. & Mrs. Daniel Kao (高光民), Dr. & Mrs. C. C. Chen (陳昭俊), Mr. & Mrs. Norman Hsu (許彬), Dr. & Mrs. Isiah Lee (李宗派), Dr. & Mrs. Joseph T. C. Lu (盧俊哲), Mr. & Mrs. Morris Chen (陳茂雄), Mr. & Mrs. George Chen (陳進琛), Dr. & Mrs. Sze-Ya Yeh (葉思雅), Mr. & Mrs. Wang Chun Hsiung (王春雄), Dr. & Mrs. Jang Yan Wu (吳政彥), Dr. Wen-Cho Yang (楊哲), Dr. & Mrs. Justin Chen (陳有義), Meiling Lai (賴美玲), Michael Chen (陳明章), and others
UPCUSA support: Pastors and elders from the United Presbyterian Church system, including San Francisco Theological Seminary, the General Assembly of the United Presbyterian Church, the Southern California/Hawaii Presbytery, and the Pacific Presbytery
Organizing Pastor:  Chaolong Kao (高昭龍) — called by Presbytery of Los Angeles Southwest in September 1971 (former TTCS Assistant Professor; Visiting Scholar at Harvard). Distinct from co-founder Dr. Daniel Kao (高光民).

Theological Vision
Dr. Albert S. Lai, who participated in the founding and later wrote his doctoral dissertation on the church, articulated a vision that transcended the church being merely a haven for immigrants. FPCLA was intended to become a “mission base” in the local community — a missional community that would witness to the gospel in the larger society.

Primary source: Toward A Community of Hope (work & sources)
Full text (GitHub): complete extract · fact sheet

Founding Process: A Detailed Account
The First Experimental Worship (August 1970)
On August 9, 1970, Reverend Jonah Chang (張瑞雄), a former minister of the Presbyterian Church of Formosa then serving at the United Methodist Church in Fresno, California, led the first experimental Sunday worship service for Formosan Christians in Los Angeles. Twenty-two adults and eleven children attended — a turnout that exceeded expectations and confirmed the viability of a dedicated Formosan congregation. Over the following four weeks, the experimental church drew growing numbers, culminating in a strong conviction among the majority that a permanent church fellowship was essential.
From Prayer Circle to Congregation
Before the church was formally organized, a spontaneous circle of 20 to 30 Formosan Christians had been meeting every other Saturday night in rotating homes throughout early 1970. This prayer meeting circle — some members previously associated with the First Evangelical Chinese Church — chose Saturday nights specifically so that those already affiliated with Sunday churches could also participate. The group made plans, held discussions, and laid the groundwork for the church’s organization.
In August 1970, Rev. Chang’s one-month experimental church served as the catalyst. When the experiment concluded at the end of August and Rev. Chang returned to Fresno, the congregation envisioned the importance of carrying on the fellowship and decided to organize a church — despite having no pastor and no outside financial support. With the assistance of Centenary United Methodist Church and its minister, Rev. Peter Chen, they used the Wesley Hall facilities of Centenary United Methodist Church until they moved to Wilshire Crest Presbyterian Church in July 1971.
UPCUSA Connection and Presbytery Approval
The Presbyterian Church of Formosa was the largest and only financially independent denomination on the island, and most members of the new church were proud Presbyterians. From the beginning, they seriously considered association with the United Presbyterian Church in the USA (UPCUSA). Through continuous contact with the Synod Office of Southern California and the Presbytery of Los Angeles Southwest, the Formosan Christian Church decided in February 1971 to join the UPCUSA and requested financial and moral support.
The Presbytery Committee voted on March 27, 1971, to work with the church leadership to develop a plan for a self-supporting United Presbyterian congregation within three to five years. A formal funding request submitted on April 14, 1971, stated: “The present request is for support of what the Committee feels to be already a highly significant ministry and mission that offers promise of becoming a successful model by a somewhat different form of church development with ethnic minorities within our Synod.”
The Presbytery of Los Angeles Southwest approved the proposed organization of the Formosan Presbyterian Church on September 28, 1971, at a meeting held at Brentwood Presbyterian Church. The Presbytery Committee concluded that “this group has a valid and viable mission.” Reverend Dr. Charles C.L. Kao (Chaolong Kao, 高昭龍) — a native Formosan, former Assistant Professor at Tainan Theological College, and then Visiting Scholar at Harvard University — was called as the organizing minister in September 1971. (Not the co-founder Dr. Daniel Kao / 高光民.)
The Presbytery’s Strategic Rationale
The Presbytery Committee identified two areas compelling their support: (1) a growing emphasis on investing church resources where there already existed a significant “spark of life” in the people to be served, and (2) the Presbytery’s intent to be responsive to changing urban demographics. The proposed congregation was consistent with Synod and General Assembly guidelines because it:

Served a clearly defined community with needs peculiar to Formosan immigrants
Included a strong corporate ministry encompassing both Christians and non-Christians
Kept open options for changing ministry styles without burdening the congregation with building concerns
Emphasized interdependence with other congregations and programs of the Synod and General Assembly

The Presbytery also recognized that a ministry to Formosan Presbyterians and the opportunity to reach non-Christian Formosans with the Gospel could not be realized apart from a Formosan church, and that effective unity of the church could be enhanced as new United Presbyterians actively participated in denominational life.
Proposed Budget (1971–1974)
The church’s leadership developed a four-year budget projection reflecting the expectation of gradual self-support:













































YearPledgesLoose OfferingSpecial DayChurch SchoolTotal Income1971$3,750$2,800$550$240$7,3401972$4,000$2,900$600$250$7,7501973$5,550$3,400$800$250$10,0001974$7,000$4,500$1,200$300$13,000
Total projected expenses (including ministerial support, Christian education, housing, car allowance, pension, administration, utilities, activities, and general mission) matched income projections, with the Presbytery and Synod of Southern California expected to cover the gap until self-support was achieved.
Membership Profile (September 1971)





























CategoryCountMembers (single / married)37 (5 / 32)Non-members (single / married)49 (15 / 28)Children33Contributing families15Potential contributing families15
The occupational profile of members and non-members reflected the highly educated nature of the community: 19 engineers, 17 students, 10 laboratory researchers, 8 in business, 6 in computer science, 5 medical doctors, 5 social workers, and 10 in other professions.
Sunday morning worship attendance averaged between 70 and 90 (including 15–20 children), with half being non-Christians searching for fellowship and the enlightenment of Christian faith. The church was attracting new attendees at a rate of 2–5 persons weekly.
Mission and Community Role
In early Taiwanese immigrant life, FPCLA functioned as:

Worship community in the mother tongue: Taiwanese-language worship for immigrants, with Sunday morning services in Formosan language
Social support network: Assistance for new arrivals navigating life in America, including immigration, employment, and health consultation
Space for identity negotiation: A place where Taiwanese immigrants could negotiate faith, identity, and public belonging
Missional community: A beacon of hope and witness to the gospel in the larger society
Spiritual anchor: A familiar place amid cultural transition, linguistic barriers, and identity uncertainty
Cultural center: Saturday afternoon open church providing facilities for table tennis, volleyball, games, music, and folk dancing

Church Activities
The church designed its activities around the fundamental needs of the community and individuals:

Sunday worship service in Formosan language, with 70–90 average attendance
Joint worship with Wilshire Crest United Presbyterian Church on the last Sunday of every month, cooperated by pastors of both congregations
Agape Meal potluck lunch after each Sunday service, featuring native food
Sunday School with 15–20 students in three classes (preschool through sixth grade)
Choir of about 15 members, practicing hymns, classics, and Formosan folk songs
Saturday afternoon open church as a social center for the entire Formosan community
Family prayer meetings every other Friday night at members’ homes, with Bible study, theological textbook study, and discussion of Christian living
Monthly lectures on topics such as “Computer and Modern Man,” “How to Find a Doctor If You Are Sick,” and “Income Tax and You,” open to the entire community
Retreats, including a successful Christmas retreat at Lazy-W Ranch with 70 adults and children

Theological Vision
Dr. Albert S. Lai, who participated in the founding and later wrote his doctoral dissertation on the church, articulated a vision that transcended the church being merely a haven for immigrants. FPCLA was intended to become a “mission base” in the local community — a missional community that would witness to the gospel in the larger society. The church was seen as a place where people could “touch one another’s heart and feel that they are one in Holy Spirit,” and where people could be “touched by the proclamation of the Gospel and be sent to serve the world.”
Historical Significance
First Taiwanese Church in North America
FPCLA was the first Taiwanese Presbyterian church established in North America, setting a precedent for subsequent Taiwanese Presbyterian churches across the continent. Over 40 Taiwanese Presbyterian churches would be established in North America in the decades following FPCLA’s founding.
Foundation for PC(USA) Connection
By establishing FPCLA under the UPCUSA/PC(USA) system, the founders created a connection with Presbyterian churches around the world, maximizing strength to care for the future of Taiwanese people. This connection resonated with church headquarters in New York, including the UPCUSA, National Council of Churches (NCC), and World Council of Churches (WCC) in Geneva.
Dissertation and Legacy
FPCLA was the central case study in Dr. Albert S. Lai’s 1971 doctoral dissertation Toward A Community of Hope — A Mission to Formosan Community in Los Angeles, which documented the church’s struggles, aspirations, and theological vision. The dissertation was reprinted in 2025 with a 50th anniversary foreword.
Theological Framework
”Internal Integration and External Harmony”
Dr. Albert S. Lai’s dissertation articulated a theological vision centered on the concept of “internal integration and external harmony” — a framework for understanding how the church could serve Formosan immigrants while maintaining their cultural identity. This concept was drawn from both psychology and theology.
Internal Integration refers to the degree of integration as a dynamic, process-oriented concept rather than a static state. It draws on Jung’s “individuation,” Maslow’s “self-actualization,” Allport’s “functional autonomy,” and Erickson’s “ego-identity.” Erich Fromm’s positive view of self-love and Paul Tillich’s “courage to be oneself” informed this understanding. For Formosan immigrants, internal integration meant:

Maintaining cultural identity while adapting to American society
Finding spiritual meaning beyond work and family
Developing a sense of belonging in a foreign land
Achieving the “courage to be oneself” — not being completely lost in a strange culture
Becoming an independent, autonomous self capable of accepting new experiences, digesting them, and integrating them into a new identity

External Harmony refers to the relationship between the individual and the broader society. It is the integration and harmony between two polarities — “one-in-two” and “two-in-one.” This meant:

Engaging with American society while maintaining distinctiveness
Building bridges between Formosan culture and American culture
Serving as a missional community in the local context
Contributing to the broader society while preserving unique identity

The source of internal integration and external harmony is love — encompassing self-love, love-for-other, agape-eros, familial love, human-heartedness, compassion, and productive love. Without love, there is no sense of security; without security, no trust; without trust, no peace of heart. “God is love” is thus theologically central: with love, internal wounds are healed, conflicts resolved, and the disintegrated person becomes whole.
From “Melting Pot” to Pluralistic Society
The dissertation examined the historical context of immigrant integration in America, contrasting two models:

The “Melting Pot” theory: Insisted European immigrants should become amalgamated or assimilated into U.S. society as fast as humanly possible by “becoming like us.” No immigrant community was encouraged to assert its group identity or cultural integrity.
Segregation and exclusion: Oriental immigrants (Chinese, Japanese, and by extension Formosans) were treated differently — expected to remain “alien” under the Oriental Exclusion Act of 1924, kept segregated, and forced to remain foreigners regardless of how long they lived in the U.S.

Lai argued that neither a racially divided America nor a culturally homogenized America was truly desirable. A pluralistic America, in which “every ethnic group is accepted for what it is and encouraged to become an integral part of U.S. society while maintaining its own group identity,” was the ideal.
The distinction between “accepted by Americans” and “to become American” was crucial: the former meant being accepted as a Formosan, while the latter meant no longer being Formosan. Formosans wanted to be treated like Americans but not to live culturally in American style — they wanted acceptance without assimilation.
The Church as “Community of Hope”
The vision for FPCLA was not merely to be a haven for immigrants, but to become a community of hope — a theological concept drawn from multiple sources:
Hope as Possibility: Hope involves three basic ideas: what one hopes for, one does not yet have or see; it may be difficult, but it is possible. Hope is neither passive waiting nor unrealistic forcing. To hope means to be ready at every moment for that which is not yet born, and not to become desperate if there is no birth in one’s lifetime.
Hope as Adventure: Gabriel Marcel spoke of “hoping” (the verb) rather than “hope” (the noun) — a psychic activity, a real occurrence in a concrete setting. Hoping occurs when a person is visited by calamity, caught by the human condition. As Roy W. Fairchild remarked: “Hope allows one to live in uncertainty… the hoping person sees reality as open-ended and not fixed, assumes that reality has resources which are as yet undiscovered and untapped. This is his risk and his adventure.”
Hope as Sharing: Hope is basically a sharing experience requiring a responsive other. Isolation leads to hopelessness and disintegration. Marcel stressed that true hoping requires an interpersonal context. Theologically, hope is the Holy Spirit in the Christian Church — “Without the experience of the Spirit, there is no distinctly Christian understanding of hope; and even if Jesus had spoken much about it, it would have signified little beyond what Judaism already understood.” Christian Church is a Community of Hope. Without hope, there will never have been such a thing as ‘Christian Church.’
The God of Promise: Christian hope is grounded in the God of promise — the God of exodus in the Old Testament and the God of resurrection in the New Testament. The church is not the Kingdom of God but a community of hope. It is a “moving church” — moving toward the future, the eschatological “Kingdom of God.” As Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote: “To be a Christian does not mean to be religious in a particular way… But to be a Christian is to be a man. It is not some religious act that makes a Christian what he is, but participation in the suffering of God in the life of the world.”
Ekklesia as “Called Out”: The term “ekklesia” indicates that the “chosen” are in no way to be called into or stay in the shelter of any organized community, but rather out of their customary attachment and security, out of the world. To follow Christ is to venture out of tradition, out of consensus of opinion, out of any comfortable settling down.
Formosan Identity and Independence: A Theological Reading
The dissertation addressed the complex political identity of Formosans through a theological lens:
National Independence — Political: The Formosan Independence Movement was fundamentally a self-preservation movement of the island’s 14 million people willing neither to be ruled by the Chinese Communists nor to be destroyed by the Chinese Nationalist regime. The vast majority of Formosans in the U.S. hoped to remain abroad until their home island became a democratic republic safe from both Nationalist and Communist rule.
Personal Independence — Psychological: Drawing on Yukichi Fukuzawa’s insight that “when a person is independent, a nation is independent,” Lai argued that spiritual and mental independence of the person and political independence of the nation are indivisible. Only when independent persons participate in nation-building can the nation itself attain independence.
Ethnos as a Vital Dimension: Every ethnic group builds up its own unique identity. Formosan study should be separated from Chinese study, since modern Formosan is very different from Chinese in terms of cultural experience and political interests. Formosan peculiarities should not be disregarded.
Colonialism and Alienation: Drawing on liberation theology (particularly Paulo Freire’s concepts), Lai described how Formosans experienced a “colonial relationship” in which the powerful dominated and controlled the lives of the weak and powerless. Formosan consciousness was “domesticated by the situation” — unable to be the subject, deprived of a sense of direction and of historical vocation. They were not simply without freedom; they were made without-freedom.
Hope as the Basis of the Independence Movement: Lai observed that “according to percentage there are more Christians than non-Christians involved in the Formosan Independence Movement.” He concluded that “the phenomenon was from a Biblical Hope Movement” — Formosan activists identified contemporary Formosan history with the Israelite Exodus, and identified themselves with biblical characters such as Abraham, Moses, Joshua, and Jesus. The theology of hope was, in his analysis, the driving force behind the political movement.
The Church’s Role in Identity Negotiation
The church served as a space where Formosan immigrants could negotiate their identity on multiple levels:

Between Formosa and America: Formosans in the U.S. were “even more Formosan than Formosans in Formosa” — they began to appreciate their folk music, kept their home-town newspapers, and searched for identity in their cultural heritage
Between Christians and non-Christians: Half of church attendees were non-Christians searching for fellowship and the enlightenment of Christian faith
Between integration and differentiation: The church affirmed that “without differentiation, there is no integration” — cultural integrity required both maintaining identity and engaging with the broader society
Between the personal and the political: The church provided a space where the political tensions of the independence movement could be held alongside spiritual formation

Good Shepherd Taiwanese Presbyterian Church
Good Shepherd Taiwanese Presbyterian Church (好牧者臺灣基督長老教會, GSTPC) is a Taiwanese-language Presbyterian congregation in Monterey Park, Southern California. The church describes itself as a Gospel-Sharing, Truth-Practicing Community—a fellowship that shares the gospel of Christ and practices biblical teaching. Members include immigrants and students from Taiwan who gather in the familiar warmth of Taiwanese (臺語) worship, with ministries for English-speaking youth and children as well.
Identity Snapshot

Chinese name: 好牧者臺灣基督長老教會
Type: Taiwanese Presbyterian congregation (PC(USA) network context)
Location: 606 South Atlantic Blvd., Monterey Park, CA 91754
Denomination / language: Presbyterian; primary worship in Taiwanese; integrated English ministry (Noah’s Ark) for youth and children
Leadership: Rev. Ming Yuan Hsu (許明遠牧師) (full-time pastor, July 2019–present per official profile)
Official site: GSTPC Official Site

Overview
GSTPC sits in Monterey Park, a hub for Chinese and Taiwanese communities in the San Gabriel Valley. The congregation formed around brothers and sisters who immigrated or studied in Southern California from Taiwan. Worship emphasizes prayer, praise, restoration of relationship with God, the Spirit’s presence, spiritual character, and equipping members to share and witness to the gospel in daily life.
The church welcomes new immigrants, students, visitors, seekers, and believers looking for a Bible-centered church family.
Vision and Mission
Per the church’s vision statement (異象使命):

Gospel Sharing Truth Practicing Community — We at Good Shepherd Taiwanese Presbyterian Church are a Gospel-Sharing, Truth-Practicing Community. 好牧者台灣基督長老教會是一個分享基督福音，遵行聖經教訓的屬靈團契。

History
Founding
GSTPC was founded by a community of Chinese immigrants and international students from Taiwan who settled in the San Gabriel Valley. Seeking to maintain their linguistic and cultural heritage while practicing their faith, they established a congregation that worships in Taiwanese (臺語), the mother tongue many Taiwanese grew up with. The church’s location in Monterey Park—a well-known center for Chinese and Taiwanese communities in Southern California—places it at the heart of this diaspora community’s daily life.
25th Anniversary (2016)
The church celebrated its 25th anniversary with a commemorative booklet (GSTPC25), documenting a quarter century of ministry, pastoral leadership, and community growth.
40th Anniversary (2021)
In December 2021, GSTPC marked its 40th anniversary with a special感恩紀念刋 (thanksgiving commemorative edition) titled 上帝的引導，雲彩見證篇 (God’s Guidance, Clouds Bear Witness). The 40th anniversary flipbook eBook (GSTPC40) includes sections on English Ministry, STM Taiwan, and the church’s 40-year narrative of God’s faithfulness. The subtitle of the publication reads: 好牧者感恩四十 — 上帝的疼惜，四十年的恩典 (Good Shepherd Gives Thanks for Forty — God’s Cherishing, Forty Years of Grace).
Pastoral Succession (歷任牧者)
Rev. Ming Yuan Hsu (許明遠牧師) has served as the church’s full-time pastor since July 2019. The church’s 40th anniversary flipbook includes a dedicated section on the history of its pastors (歷任牧者), tracing the pastoral lineage across four decades. GSTPC’s public materials also preserve memorial and historical posts, including remembrance services for prior pastoral leaders.
Connection to Monterey Park Community
Monterey Park is widely recognized as one of the earliest and most established Chinese suburban communities in the United States. GSTPC’s presence in this community provides a spiritual anchor for Taiwanese and Chinese immigrants, students, and families navigating life in Southern California while maintaining connections to their Taiwanese heritage and faith.
Ministries
GSTPC offers a range of ministries serving different age groups and needs within the congregation:

Noah’s Ark English ministry — Truth and life teaching for second-generation youth and children growing up in the U.S. This program was added in recent years to more deeply pass on the Christian faith to the immigrant second generation.
Adult Sunday school — Weekly Bible study and instruction for adults.
Choir — Regular gathering and practice for the church choir.
活泉 (Living Spring) fellowship — Senior member fellowship for older adults.
Sisters’ fellowship — Women’s ministry and small group gatherings.
Area home small groups — Weekday neighborhood-based small group Bible study and fellowship.
Discipleship training (門徒訓練) — Discipleship equipment program (listed as paused through March 2026; times subject to change).
Student fellowship / QT Bible study — Friday evening student fellowship and Quiet Time Bible study (listed as paused through March 2026; times subject to change).

Worship and Programs

Sunday worship (in person / live stream): Sundays 10:00 AM–11:00 AM — unified family worship with English ministry and children’s ministry during the same block (worship live).
Wednesday prayer meeting: Weekly midweek prayer gathering (prayer meeting).
Sunday school (children): Sundays 10:00 AM–11:30 AM — Bible time, crafts, music, and activities (children’s ministry).
Digital bulletins: Weekly bulletins and sermon listings on the bulletin archive.

Notable Events
馬偕博士台灣宣教150週年紀念主日 (2022)
On March 6, 2022, GSTPC participated in the joint worship service commemorating the 150th anniversary of Dr. James L. Maxwell (馬偕博士)‘s missionary work in Taiwan (馬偕博士台灣宣教150週年紀念主日). This was an outdoor worship service celebrating 150 years of Presbyterian missionary presence in Taiwan, connecting GSTPC’s heritage to the broader story of the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan.
TPC 50th Anniversary Special (May–June 2020)
GSTPC hosted the Rev. David Huang (黃德利牧師) for the TPC 50th Anniversary Special Program (TPC 50 週年特別節目), a multi-episode broadcast celebrating 50 years of the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan. Three episodes were published:

Since 2020, Rev. Ming Yuan Hsu (許明遠牧師) has published daily spiritual reflections (靈修默想 / 每日靈修) on the church website. The archive contains approximately 123 entries from 2020 alone, published regularly throughout the year. These devotionals are accessible via the Devotion Archive.

Irvine Taiwanese Presbyterian Church (爾灣台灣基督長老教會 / ITPC)
Summary
Irvine Taiwanese Presbyterian Church (ITPC, 爾灣台灣基督長老教會) is a Taiwanese-language Presbyterian congregation in Orange County, California, affiliated with the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan (PCT, 台灣基督長老教會). Founded around 2012, the church serves a community of Taiwanese immigrants and retirees in the Irvine and Laguna Woods area who have relocated from across the United States. The congregation worships at the chapel of Geneva Presbyterian Church, located at 24301 El Toro Rd, Laguna Hills, CA 92637.

History
ITPC was established around 2012 as a Taiwanese-language congregation for immigrants and retirees in the Southern California area, particularly in Irvine and Laguna Woods Village. The church found a home through a partnership with Geneva Presbyterian Church, which opened its chapel for ITPC’s worship services. The community consists largely of Taiwanese-born retirees who relocated to the area after retiring from careers across the United States.
The church has maintained a continuous presence for over a decade, celebrating its 515th anniversary with a commemorative booklet in 2023. The congregation has grown from a small gathering to a community of approximately 120 members who worship in the Taiwanese (Hokkien/台语) language each Sunday.
In August 2025, Rev. Li Fu-Jen (李輔仁牧師) began his pastoral ministry at ITPC, succeeding Rev. Chen Meihui (陳美蕙) and Rev. Zhang Xuanxin (張宣信), who had served the congregation in various capacities over the years.

Leadership
Current Pastor: Rev. Li Fu-Jen (李輔仁牧師)
Rev. Li Fu-Jen began his pastoral ministry at ITPC in August 2025. He brings a unique background that bridges technical engineering and theological education.
Early Life and Conversion:
Li Fu-Jen was born into a non-religious but loving family as the sixth of seven siblings. His father was a self-made businessman who studied at Waseda University’s electrical engineering department in Japan. His mother was a daughter of the 台北六張犁黃家 (Huang family of Liuzhangli), a prominent Taiwanese Christian family. Despite the family’s lack of formal religious affiliation, both parents provided a nurturing environment with considerable freedom.
As a child, he occasionally attended Sunday services and youth fellowship at Taipei Chengjian Christian Presbyterian Church (台北建成基督長老教會) with his elder sister. His conversion occurred during his second year of high school at Tamsui High School, when a primary school classmate convinced him to attend a summer camp — where, on the final day, he responded to the pastor’s call and committed his life to Christ. His deeper faith reflection began during his final year at Tunghai University, as he sought God’s guidance for his uncertain future.
Engineering Career:
After university graduation, Rev. Li spent 15 years working as a mechanical engineer at an aerospace company in the United States. During this period, his faith underwent a profound transformation. Through God’s mercy, he re-evaluated the meaning and purpose of his life and ultimately responded to God’s call to full-time ministry.
Theological Training:
Beginning in 1997, Rev. Li pursued theological education at evangelical seminaries, including 正道神學院, Fuller Theological Seminary, and Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary. He was ordained in 2004 after completing seminary.
Ministry Career:
After ordination, Rev. Li served in evangelical churches and organizations in Los Angeles, then moved to Houston, and returned to Los Angeles, always within evangelical church contexts. In August 2025, he came to ITPC to serve as pastor, describing it as another experience of God’s special grace.
Family:
Rev. Li’s wife is a fifth-generation Christian who met and married him at a church in Los Angeles. Before and after Rev. Li entered ministry, she has been his greatest helper — dedicating herself to family, supporting his seminary studies through her own work, and exercising spiritual gifts in musical ministry. Her calling has taken her to Houston, Los Angeles, Taiwan, China, and Eastern Malaysia for music ministry.
They have two adult children: their daughter works at a kindergarten in Houston, and their son works in Tokyo, pursuing his passion for animation. Though separated across three cities, the family maintains a weekly video call every Saturday morning for fellowship and prayer.

Mission Statement
ITPC’s mission is articulated through nine guiding principles drawn from Scripture:

尊主為大 (Great is the Lord) — Colossians 3:15
永生神的家 (The household of the living God) — Hebrews 3:6
心靈和誠實敬拜 (Worship in Spirit and in Truth) — John 4:23
學像基督 (Become like Christ) — Ephesians 4:13
研讀聖經 (Study the Bible humbly and seriously) — 1 Timothy 4:15-17
愛人如己 (Love your neighbor as yourself) — Matthew 22:39
相愛合一 (Enjoy loving, united fellowship) — John 13:34-35
承擔大使命 (Embrace the Great Commission) — Matthew 28:19-20
金灯台 (Golden Lampstand) — Revelation 1:20 — “We hope to become a lampstand in this community, so that all people may be blessed through us” (Genesis 12:2-3)


Ministries & Programs
ITPC offers a comprehensive range of ministries and programs serving the spiritual, educational, and social needs of its Taiwanese community:
主日崇拜 (Sunday Worship)

Time: Sunday 10:00 AM
Language: Taiwanese (台语/Hokkien)
Location: Geneva Presbyterian Church Chapel, 24301 El Toro Rd, Laguna Hills, CA 92637
Attendance: Approximately 120 members
Live Stream: Available via YouTube (enter at 9:50 AM on Sunday mornings)
Sermon recordings and church bulletins are published weekly and archived on the church website

電腦教室 (Computer Class)
A non-religious community service offering digital literacy training for seniors, taught primarily in Taiwanese with Chinese and English technical terms.
Features:

Taiwanese-language instruction
Small class sizes (under 10 students)
Hands-on practice with immediate instructor support
No tuition — only a small registration/materials fee

Courses offered (each 5-6 weeks, once per week, 90 minutes):


PC101: Basic computer skills (5 weeks) — hardware/software overview, desktop, mouse, Windows 7, Chinese input, Internet basics, email


PC201: Chinese input methods and file management (5 weeks)


PC205: Microsoft Word (5 weeks) — professional document creation and editing


PC206: Microsoft PowerPoint (5 weeks) — creating professional presentations with text, images, graphics, and video


PC208: Picasa (5 weeks) — photo import, organization, editing, email sharing, slideshows, CD/DVD creation


PC305: Website building and maintenance (6 weeks) — XHTML, CSS, domain registration, hosting, FTP


iPad101: Basic iPad functions (5 weeks) — navigation, settings, Safari, email, App Store, camera, photos


iPad201: Photo organization and editing (5 weeks) — Camera, Photos, iPhoto


iPad205: Application software (5 weeks) — Dropbox, Notability, Skype, LINE, etc.

He served as a chemistry professor, computer science professor, and department chair with over 35 years of university teaching experience. He is now an emeritus professor at Louisiana State University Southeast and volunteers with ITPC and Tustin Presbyterian Church on IT infrastructure.
長青教室 (Senior Class) — Flagship Lecture Program
The 長青教室 (Senior Class) is ITPC’s flagship educational program — a weekly lecture series for seniors featuring talks by professors, doctors, engineers, pastors, and community leaders. With 100+ regular attendees, it has become a cornerstone of the Taiwanese community in Orange County.

organizations/national-taiwanese-presbyt.content:
National Taiwanese Presbyterian Council (NTPC)
National Taiwanese Presbyterian Council (NTPC) is an organization of Taiwanese Presbyterian churches in the United States, operating under the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) [PC(USA)] system. The NTPC plays a key role in preserving Taiwanese Presbyterian heritage and supporting diaspora church communities.
Identity Snapshot

Type: Presbyterian church council/organization
Geography: United States
Denomination: Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) [PC(USA)]
Focus: Taiwanese-American Presbyterian ministry, church heritage preservation, diaspora support

Historical Role
FPCLA Founding Connection
The NTPC traces its roots to the founding of the first Taiwanese Presbyterian church in North America — the Formosan Presbyterian Church in Los Angeles (FPCLA) — in 1970. FPCLA was established under the United Presbyterian Church in the USA (UPCUSA, now PC(USA)) system, and the NTPC grew from this foundation to become a national council of Taiwanese Presbyterian churches.
50th Anniversary Context (2024–2025)
In 2024, NTPC celebrated its 50th anniversary; Rev. David Huang edited a commemorative publication. In 2025 the Annual Conference theme was “Preserving and Passing On the Faith History of NTPC,” and the council established the NTPC Historical Committee.
Mission and Vision
The NTPC’s work is guided by the theological vision articulated in Dr. Albert S. Lai’s dissertation Toward A Community of Hope — that the church should transcend being merely a haven for immigrants and become a missional community, a beacon of hope and witness to the gospel in the larger society.
NTPC Historical Committee (2025–Present)
Establishment
Rev. Ching Fang Chen (陳清芳) was appointed inaugural chairperson of the NTPC Historical Committee in 2025, stating:

“The history of the Church is a testament to the grace of God—a record not only of divine providence but of the fellowship, labor, and witness of God’s people through the ages. Half a century has passed in the blink of an eye. Many of the pioneering stories and tear-stained testimonies of those who sowed in faith are at risk of fading as the generations who lived them grow old and pass on. Without timely preservation, these precious memories may be lost to time.”

Mission and Purpose

Preserving faith history of Taiwanese American Presbyterian churches
Publishing historical resources (first publication: 2025 republication of Lai’s dissertation)
Encouraging church archives across congregations
Connecting generations through documented witness

Dissertation as Cornerstone Resource

Primary work page: Toward A Community of Hope (work & sources)
Full text (GitHub archive): complete extract · fact sheet


“Particular gratitude is due to Dr. Albert S. Lai, whose 1971 Doctor of Ministry dissertation, ‘Toward a Community of Hope — A Mission to Formosan Community in Los Angeles,’ remains a rare and invaluable document.”

The NTPC Executive Committee formally endorsed the publication.
50th Anniversary Republication (2025)
The 2025 republication of Toward A Community of Hope included:

Foreword by NTPC Moderator Dr. Yunching Yeh Davis (葉芸青): “Half a Century of Faith and Mission”
Foreword by PCT Moderator Rev. En Sheng Pan (潘恩盛)

people/albert-s-lai.content:
Dr. Albert S. Lai (賴信雄)
Dr. Albert S. Lai (賴信雄, Lai Sin-hiong) is a Taiwanese American pastor, theologian, and institution-builder who helped establish the first Taiwanese Presbyterian Church in North America and authored the landmark 1971 dissertation Toward A Community of Hope — A Mission to Formosan Community in Los Angeles, reprinted in 2025 with a 50th anniversary foreword.
Identity Snapshot

Full name: Albert S. Lai (賴信雄, Lai Sin-hiong)
Era: 1960s–2020s (active 1960s–1970s; 2025 republication at age 84+)
Geography: Taiwan → San Francisco → Los Angeles, California
Education: San Francisco Theological Seminary (doctoral dissertation); Taiwan Theological College and Seminary (TTCS)
Core roles: Pastor, theologian, seminary educator, FPCLA founding member, dissertation author

Historical Context
Dr. Lai’s life and work sit at the intersection of migration-era pastoral care and institution formation. In 1970, he participated in the founding of the Formosan Presbyterian Church in Los Angeles (FPCLA), the first Taiwanese church in North America. In 1971, he produced a doctoral dissertation that connected historical memory, migration pressure, identity tension, and communal mission. His work remains a foundational reference for Taiwanese American church history.
FPCLA Founding (1970)
Dr. Lai was among the enthusiastic believers who co-founded FPCLA under the theology and system of the United Presbyterian Church (UPCUSA, now PC(USA)). The founding involved:

Co-founders: Dr. & Mrs. Daniel Kao (高光民), Dr. & Mrs. C. C. Chen (陳昭俊), Mr. & Mrs. Norman Hsu (許彬), Dr. & Mrs. Isiah Lee (李宗派), Dr. & Mrs. Joseph T. C. Lu (盧俊哲), Mr. & Mrs. Morris Chen (陳茂雄), Mr. & Mrs. George Chen (陳進琛), Dr. & Mrs. Sze-Ya Yeh (葉思雅), Mr. & Mrs. Wang Chun Hsiung (王春雄), Dr. & Mrs. Jang Yan Wu (吳政彥), Dr. Wen-Cho Yang (楊哲), Dr. & Mrs. Justin Chen (陳有義), Meiling Lai (賴美玲), Michael Chen (陳明章), and others
Supporting pastors and elders: From the UPCUSA system including San Francisco Theological Seminary, the General Assembly of the United Presbyterian Church, the Southern California/Hawaii Presbytery, and the Pacific Presbytery
Organizing Pastor:  Chaolong Kao (高昭龍) — former TTCS faculty / Harvard Visiting Scholar; called by Presbytery of Los Angeles Southwest (Sep 1971). Distinct from co-founder Daniel Kao.
Predecessor experiment: “Taiyou Church” (太陽教會) and the Aug 1970 experimental worship led by Rev. Jonah Chang (張瑞雄)

Dissertation: Toward A Community of Hope (1971)

Primary work page: Toward A Community of Hope (work & sources)
Full text (GitHub archive): complete extract · fact sheet

Dr. Lai’s doctoral dissertation at San Francisco Theological Seminary was titled Toward A Community of Hope — A Mission to Formosan Community in Los Angeles. It was:

Theological and prophetic: Called the church to transcend being merely a haven for immigrants and become a missional community, a beacon of hope and witness to the gospel in the larger society
Six chapters: Formosan in Formosa Yesterday; Formosan in Formosa Today; Formosan in The United States; Formosan Christian Church in Los Angeles; Integration, Independence and Identity of Formosan Community; Toward a Community
Vision: The church as a “hopeful community” — not a safe retreat for insiders, but a dynamic body for the hope of the world, choosing love in adversity, service in marginality, and witness in brokenness
Significance: The first Taiwanese church in North America; FPCLA did not exist merely to bridge linguistic or cultural gaps but sought to become a “mission base” in the local community

See also the FPCLA page for Chapter IV founding timeline, budget, membership, and activities.
50th Anniversary Republication (2025)
In 2025, the dissertation was reprinted with a 50th anniversary foreword by Dr. Yunching Yeh Davis (NTPC Moderator), along with forewords from the PCT (Rev. En Sheng Pan), NTPC Historical Committee (Rev. Ching Fang Chen), Rev. Mingyuan Hsu (Good Shepherd TPC), and Rev. Pinghsi Liu (Tainan East Gate Barclay Memorial Church). The republication was published by Taiwan Church Press and the Incorporated Association of Tainan East Gate Barclay History Education Promotion.
Self-Preface (May 2025)
In his Self-Preface, Dr. Lai reflected:

“When my esteemed Rev. Mingyuan Hsu of the Los Angeles Good Shepherd Presbyterian Church in Taiwan informed me that Rev. Pinghsi Liu and his team from the Tainan East Gate Barclay Memorial Church were interested in my dissertation and wanted to translate it into Chinese for publication, I was filled with gratitude.”

He noted that existing writings about Taiwanese churches in North America all start from the 1980s, while his dissertation reflects the lives of Taiwanese and Taiwanese Christians in Southern California from the 1960s to the early 1970s — a period when Taiwan was under the Kuomintang’s White Terror, and thousands of Taiwanese students came to the US each year.
Recall the Story Behind the Dissertation
In his extended postscript written over 50 years later, Dr. Lai narrated the remarkable story of how his 1971 dissertation was rediscovered, translated, and published — a journey he could never have imagined while writing it.
Rediscovery and Publication
When the dissertation was presented to readers in 2025, Dr. Lai noted that the intended audience at the time was only about 10 people: his two thesis advisors, one project field consultant, and the seminary faculty thesis review committee. In the information-scarce 1960s, these professors had very limited understanding of Taiwan and had never heard of the Taiwanese people’s desire to “rise up” or the persecution faced by the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan.
The dissertation, presented in Chinese to Taiwanese on the island and in America more than 50 years later, was something Dr. Lai could never have imagined. It was Rev. Mingyuan Hsu of the Los Angeles Good Shepherd Presbyterian Church in Taiwan who first approached Dr. Lai, informing him that Rev. Pinghsi Liu and his team from the Tainan East Gate Barclay Memorial Church were interested in the dissertation and wanted to translate it into Chinese for publication. Dr. Lai was filled with gratitude.
The publication journey spanned from 2023 to 2025, culminating in the 50th anniversary republication by Taiwan Church Press and the Incorporated Association of Tainan East Gate Barclay History Education Promotion, with forewords from Dr. Yunching Yeh Davis (NTPC Moderator), the PCT, NTPC Historical Committee, Rev. Mingyuan Hsu, and Rev. Pinghsi Liu.
Historical Context of the Writing
Dr. Lai emphasized that the dissertation was written during one of the most tumultuous periods in modern history. As a student at San Francisco Theological Seminary from 1968 to 1972, he was immersed in the American cultural revolution — the women’s rights movement, civil rights movement, anti-Vietnam War movement, counterculture movement, the assassinations of Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert Kennedy, and the moon landing. Theology students at the time were exposed to “Feminist Theology,” “Black Theology,” “Theology of the Death of God,” “Theology of Liberation,” and “Theology of Hope.”
Simultaneously, dramatic events unfolded related to Taiwan: the expulsion of the Republic of China from the United Nations, and the April 24, 1970, incident when Peter Huang (黃文雄), a Cornell doctoral candidate, shot at Chingkuo Chiang (蔣經國) at the New York Plaza Hotel. In 1971, the ROC was expelled from the UN, and Taiwan became a “global orphan.” Nixon’s official visit to China in February 1972 further worsened Taiwan’s political situation. Dr. Lai graduated from SFTS in May 1972, during this period of profound disorientation.
Chapter VI: Toward a Community of Hope
Chapter VI of Dr. Lai’s dissertation developed the theological framework that gave the project its name. The chapter explored hope not as passive waiting but as active, shared venture — and the church as the community where hope is generated and sustained.
Hope Is Possibility
Dr. Lai defined hope as the recognition that what one hopes for is not yet possessed but is possible. He drew on Gabriel Marcel’s distinction between “hope” (the noun) and “hoping” (the verb), arguing that hoping is a psychic activity that occurs only when a person feels “caught” by the human condition — in captivity. Only when everything does not go perfectly well can hoping enter the picture.
He noted the increase in despair and “un-hope” among Formosan people in the United States, especially after Nixon’s shift on China policy. The word “hopeless” was often used by Formosans to stand for “helplessness” on one hand and “fearfulness” on the other — an inability to visualize a future in which personal identity and national independence were possible.
Hope Is Adventure
Citing Gabriel Marcel’s Homo Viator, Dr. Lai argued that hoping is a process — a psychic activity of the person, not just an idea. He quoted Roy W. Fairchild: “Hope allows one to live in uncertainty. Hope cannot predict that such and such will happen, nor claim that such and such must happen. But because the hoping person sees reality as open-ended and not fixed, he assumes that reality has resources which are as yet undiscovered and untapped. This is his risk and his adventure.”
Hope Is Sharing
A central thesis of Chapter VI was that hope is fundamentally a sharing experience. Dr. Lai wrote: “Often hope is considered an interior strength, some believe one possesses alone. But can one hope as a lone individual? … Hope is basically a sharing experience. It requires a responsive other if one is to discover real hope.”
He cited Marcel’s insight that true hoping requires an interpersonal context, and isolation leads to hopelessness and disintegration. “For human beings, mutual help is part of the nature of hope; hope is the anticipation of helpful relationship. Hope grows in a network of human caring. Theologically speaking, hope is the Holy Spirit in the Christian Church. Without the experience of the Spirit, there is no distinctly Christian understanding of hope.”
The Church as Community of Hope
Dr. Lai’s ecclesiology placed the church squarely as a “community of hope” — not a Community of the Past, not merely a Community of the Now, and not even a Community of the Future. “For hope is historical,” he wrote. “Michael Novak is right when he says, ‘To be a Christian is to be a member of historical people.’ So accordingly, hope is not to be mistaken for a futurism that flees from the burden and the joys of the present. It is not an escapist trick; it is not creating a new ‘God of the gaps’ so that we merely slip into the future the problems we cannot solve in the present. If anything, it calls us to the front line of world history as the missionary people of God.”
He drew on Dietrich Bonhoeffer’s vision of Christian life as participation in the suffering of God in the life of the world, and on Robert Lee’s conclusion that “the Christian is armed with hope and confidence, born of realism and the realization that we are temporary and fallen residents of this earth.”
Dr. Lai also drew a powerful parallel between the Formosan experience and the Israelite Exodus: “Like the Israelites of old, they search for the meaning of life. Probably this is why among Formosans, according to percentage, there are more Christians committed to the Formosan Independence Movement than non-Christians — since the phenomenon of the Formosan Independence Movement logically is a Hope Movement.”
The “Out” of Hope
Dr. Lai explored the radical implication of ekklesia — the “called-out” nature of the Christian community. To follow Christ is to venture “out of tradition, out of ‘consensus of opinion,’ out of any comfortable settling down in the shelter of the anonymous mass.” He warned against the common error of mistaking the symbol for reality — “one only looks at the finger which points out the way and then prefers to suck it comfortably, instead of following the direction it indicates.”
Conclusion: Lessons from History
Dr. Lai’s conclusion synthesized the dissertation’s critical findings across multiple dimensions:
Formosan Nationalism and Hope
Dr. Lai observed that historically, Formosans had been struggling for self-determination and national independence for almost thirty years without success. “The future of Formosan independence lies mainly in the hand of the majority itself. The real test of nationalism is a people’s willingness to fight for it. In other words, when a person is independent, a nation is independent. Realistic and dynamic hope is the key to the problems of independence, personal and national as well.”
Ethnic Church Mission
He argued that new immigrants from Formosa should not be treated as regular immigrants but as people with particular problems requiring specific pastoral care. “The goal of a church is to carry out Christian mission, not to self-support. This is especially true to a new ethnic church. Ministry concerns primarily people (person) not head-counting or real estates. The church is where a group of people can touch one another’s heart and feel they are one in the Holy Spirit.”
Experience Over Theory
Dr. Lai emphasized attending to actual experience over abstract theory: “In principle, it seems good to attend more closely to our actual experience than to theories, formulas or doctrine which purports to articulate and to direct that experience. For experience is in principle richer, more complex, and more full of compass.”
The Biblical Hope Movement
A striking conclusion was his observation that “according to percentage there are much more Christians than non-Christians involved in the Formosan Hope Movement — Formosan Independence Movement.” He concluded that this phenomenon stemmed from a Biblical Hope Movement, with Formosan activists identifying contemporary history with the Israelite Exodus and identifying themselves with Abraham, Moses, Joshua, and Jesus.
Hope vs. Hopelessness
Dr. Lai articulated a crucial distinction: “It is when we mix hope with what is hopeless that we become filled with hopelessness. It is the recognition that some ways are hopeless that open up for us the way to find hope. The important thing is not to think that all things can be hoped for but to keep the hopeless out of hope, to separate the impossible from the possible.”
He quoted Paul Freire: “This climate of hope is born at the exact moment when a given society begins to turn upon itself and finds out that it is not finished, that there is an infinite number of tasks to be accomplished. The hopelessness and pessimism which existed before about its present and future, as well as the naïve optimism, give place to a critical optimism, to hope.”
The Missing 50 Years: Dr. Lai’s Personal Journey
The “Missing 50 Years” section traces Dr. Lai’s extraordinary life after completing his doctorate in May 1972 — a period during which he largely disappeared from public Taiwanese church circles.
Graduation and Disappearance
Dr. Lai completed his doctoral degree in May 1972. Pastor Chaolong Kao specially flew to San Francisco Theological Seminary to attend the graduation ceremony. In July 1972, Dr. Lai’s fiancée, Jane Hatsuko Ueno (a third-generation Japanese-American from Hawaii), and he held their wedding ceremony at FPCLA, officiated by Pastor Kao — the first wedding held after the establishment of the Los Angeles Presbyterian Church.
After that, Dr. Lai disappeared from the Taiwanese church community. He explained that theological education taught him that after a pastor hands over pastoral work to a successor, it is best not to continue attending that church, as it increases pressure on the successor. He also cited his dream of Taiwanese independence and missionary work in China — matters with “untold difficulties” during the turbulent political era.
From “Theology of Hope” to “Theology of Revolution”
The period from 1970 to 1972 was described as “the most tumultuous and terrifying time for Taiwan.” In 1970, the April 24 incident saw Peter Huang shoot at Chingkuo Chiang. In 1971, Taiwan was expelled from the UN. Nixon’s visit to China in February 1972 further worsened Taiwan’s situation.
Inspired by Nixon’s engagement with the CCP, Dr Lai believed the Taiwanese people must study the CCP to learn how to overthrow the KMT. He discovered that Mao Zedong had written articles in 1928 and 1936 supporting Taiwanese independence, and had broadcast support for Taiwanese independence from Yan’an after the February 28 Incident.
Trade with China: “Little Asia Imports”
Dr. Lai established an import company called “Little Asia Imports” (LAImports), borrowing nearly HK$20,000 from friends and family plus his own savings, to procure Chinese handicrafts for wholesale in Los Angeles. He planned to use trade as a means to establish connections with the CCP. The first year ran smoothly, but the Red Guards’ rebellion in China during the Cultural Revolution made international trade nearly impossible, and his “China Dream” ended abruptly.
Taiwan Independent Revolution Army (T.I.R.A.)
While managing his trade business, Dr. Lai joined the “Taiwan Independent Revolution Army” (T.I.R.A.), a secret underground organization founded by Su Beng (史明). He practiced shooting at a range near Highway 60 and Rosemead Boulevard every Saturday, and learned about explosives and demolition. He opened a bank account for T.I.R.A. by placing a three-day DBA advertisement in the classified section of the Los Angeles Times.
The effort came to a standstill when his comrade Kenneth Wang graduated and returned to Brazil, leaving Dr. Lai as the only person in T.I.R.A. About a year and a half later, an FBI agent visited him, having obtained his information from the bank. The agent warned him that armed revolutionary activities are not allowed in the U.S. and fall under the category of terrorist violence.
Maytai Companies and Chinese Community Yellow Pages
During the 1970s wave of Taiwanese refugees fleeing to the U.S., Dr. Lai shifted his focus. With his friend Jihsiung Chen (陳吉雄), a pioneer in international color printing in Taiwan, he founded “Maytai Companies” — the first advertising company, Chinese-language translation company, Chinese color printing factory, and Chinese photographic studio for Taiwanese people in Los Angeles.
By 1980, they established the “Chinese Community Yellow Pages” phone directory, which grew from fewer than 200 pages and 3,000 copies in its first year to nearly 3,000 pages and 100,000 copies within a few years. They later published city versions covering the top ten U.S. cities with large Chinese populations, receiving awards from the Yellow Page Publishers Association, including the Annual Achievement Gold Award.
American Business & Industry and the Nixon Connection
The company’s 1984 Los Angeles Olympic Guide Book attracted the attention of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In 1986, the company published “American Business & Industry” in Shanghai with the Shanghai Publishing Bureau. The press conference at the Jinjiang Hotel was attended by U.S. Consul General in Shanghai and then-Secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Committee Zemin Jiang (江澤民). This was reported on CCTV Evening News — the first time in history that a new book’s publication was reported in a national evening news broadcast in China.
The book featured a “Letter to the People of China” signed by former U.S. President Nixon, which made it a reference for Chinese officials during the reform and opening-up period. This led to ASM becoming the officially designated U.S. training program partner of the State Administration of Foreign Experts Affairs (SAFEA), training over 6,000 Chinese government officials and corporate executives from 1988 to 2000.
The 1996 Missile Crisis and Realization About the CCP
By 1996, when Taiwan held its first direct presidential election, the CCP’s reaction — including missile tests over Taiwan — surprised Dr. Lai. He learned that all personnel in the PLA missile unit were very nervous, worried the missiles might fall back onto Taiwan.
After the 1997 handover of Hong Kong, Dr. Lai finally realized: “In the long run, the CCP is more brutal and terrifying than the KMT for the Taiwanese people.” He gradually recognized that China did not have what he wanted — the secret to overthrowing the KMT. The CCP was not as powerful as it seemed; it was primarily the internal corruption within the KMT that pushed it to the brink.
SIAS College and “Fisherman’s Hall”
Dr. Lai shifted from government training to education, assisting his friend Chen in founding SIAS College (西亞斯學院) in Zhengzhou, Henan. He spent years commuting between Beijing and Zhengzhou, helping develop foreign resources, international student programs, and student clubs (which expanded from fewer than 20 to nearly 200 types).
He also played a key role in establishing “Fisherman’s Hall Christian Church” near SIAS College to serve the 150-180 foreign teachers hired annually. Over twenty years, the church grew from a small chapel serving foreign teachers into a magnificent seven-story building with 40 clergy and staff — far beyond his expectations.
Letting Go: COVID and the End of an Era
In mid-December 2019, Dr. Lai returned to Los Angeles from Beijing and did not return. COVID-19 led to flight suspensions lasting two to three years. During this time, he reassessed the changes in both the U.S. and China, including tightening control over universities and intensifying surveillance of Taiwanese people in China. He officially informed SIAS that he would not be going back.
By 2025, the number of foreign teachers at SIAS had dropped from 150-200 to fewer than 40-50. The party committee at SIAS had expanded from four stationed personnel to 102 party branches covering faculty and students. The U.S.-China relationship had shifted from “quasi-allies” fifty years ago to “quasi-enemies” today.
Sixty Years in America
As Dr. Lai approached completing sixty years in America, he reflected on what he called a “pendulum effect” — sixty years ago, San Francisco was in the midst of a leftist cultural revolution; in 2025, under Trump 2.0, the “MAGA wave” seemed to be resurfacing. He noted that as a passionate youth, he may not have been “far left,” but was not far from being “New Left” — the most popular phrase being “Don’t trust anyone over 30.” Now in his eighties, he found himself supporting MAGA, leaning toward the center-right.

“After careful reflection and humble introspection through prayer, I realize that this dream has not been the one I initially had. I ultimately recognize that in my life, there has always been a dream, and this dream has been realized, but it is not the same dream I started with. God’s arrangements are truly marvelous!”

Postscript: Echoes of History
The Postscript positions Dr. Lai’s dissertation as a prophetic document whose insights remain relevant fifty years later. The issues discussed — Taiwanese identity, political dilemmas, and the pursuit of hope — continue to resonate in contemporary Taiwanese society.
Echoes of History: The Shaping of Taiwanese Identity
The Postscript emphasizes that the dissertation laid the foundation for understanding the unique and complex identity of the Taiwanese people. Through colonial rule by the Dutch, Spanish, Ming and Qing dynasties, and the Japanese government, Taiwan’s history has always been closely linked to foreign influence. Japanese colonial rule (1895–1945) inadvertently contributed to “National Unity” among the Taiwanese people by severing connections with mainland China and improving living standards.
The 228 Incident (1947), estimated to have caused 15,000 to 25,000 deaths, “completely destroyed the Taiwanese people’s illusions about their ‘motherland’ and became a distant cause of the Taiwanese independence movement.” The subsequent martial law and systematic oppression, while consolidating KMT rule, inadvertently strengthened the shared identity of the Taiwanese people and drove many young individuals abroad.
From Exile to Democracy: The “Quiet Revolution”
The Postscript traces Taiwan’s democratization from the 1970s to the present: the Kaohsiung Incident (1979), the establishment of the Democratic Progressive Party (1986), the lifting of martial law (1987), the Wild Lily Movement (1990), the first direct presidential election (1996), and the completion of three transfers of power.
The “Quiet Revolution” nature of Taiwan’s democratization lies in its avoidance of large-scale bloodshed — a lesson drawn from the bloody experiences of the 228 Incident and the Kaohsiung Incident. In the eyes of believers, this peaceful transformation is a manifestation of “God’s grace.”
In 2021, the Economist Intelligence Unit ranked Taiwan eighth in its democracy index, the highest among countries outside the Western world.
A Community of Hope: Christian Faith in Times of Crisis
The Postscript concludes that the Formosan Presbyterian Church in Los Angeles was not merely a religious space but a “Mission of Identity” — providing a foundation of hope for “lost” Taiwanese, preserving and cultivating a unique Taiwanese identity abroad, and providing a platform for the Taiwanese language, culture, and shared experiences.

“This sense of ‘hope’ in Christian faith is not only an ultimate concern but also a practical force that transforms individual suffering under authoritarianism into a commitment to social change, providing a deep moral and spiritual foundation for the ‘Quiet Revolution.‘”

Conclusion: Lessons from History and the Sustainability of Democracy
Dr. Lai’s dissertation, written in 1971, is described as “not only a profound depiction of the Taiwanese people’s struggles at that time but also a prophecy for future transformation.” The journey from Taiwan’s authoritarian oppression beginning in 1945 to today’s thriving democracy is widely praised by the international community as a peaceful “Quiet Revolution” — which can also be viewed as “God’s grace.”

“Learning from history is not merely a retrospective endeavor; it is about continuously constructing a more just and free Taiwanese society, carrying on the mission embodied in ‘Toward a Community of Hope,’ and allowing the light of hope to continue shining on this land.”

Contributions and Legacy

Co-founded FPCLA (1970) — First Taiwanese church in North America, under UPCUSA/PC(USA) system
Authored Toward A Community of Hope (1971) — Foundational dissertation on Taiwanese immigrant church formation, reprinted 2025
Theological vision — Articulated church as both ethnic refuge and public mission community; “hopeful community” theology
Cross-generational reference — 2025 republication linked to NTPC, PCT, and broader Taiwanese church heritage
Seminarian mentor — Taught at TTCS where future leaders including Rev. Chaolong Kao were students

馬偕博士 (George Leslie Macdonald)
George Leslie Macdonald (馬偕, 1838–1901), commonly known in Chinese as 馬偕博士 (Dr. Maxwell), was a Canadian Presbyterian missionary, medical doctor, evangelist, and educator who spent the last 29 years of his life in northern Taiwan, profoundly shaping its religious, educational, and medical landscape.
Identity Snapshot

Full name: George Leslie Macdonald (馬偕)
Born: September 21, 1838, Tullydonnell, Ontario, Canada
Died: June 2, 1901, Tamsui, Taiwan (aged 62)
Education: Roxbury Latin School; Toronto University (MD); Toronto Missionary College
Marriage: Married Henrietta Elizabeth Runnels in 1872; they had one daughter, Emily
Role: Presbyterian medical missionary, evangelist, educator, physician
Mission field: Northern Taiwan (1872–1901)
Known as: 馬偕 (Ma Kai) in Chinese; 馬偕博士 (Dr. Maxwell) by the Taiwanese people
Legacy: Founded the Presbyterian Church in Northern Taiwan, 偕醫學堂 (Ochong Medical School), and the Tamsui Theological College (now STM Taiwan)

Life and Mission
Arrival in Taiwan
George Leslie Macdonald arrived in Tamsui (淡水), northern Taiwan, on August 23, 1872, after studying theology and medicine in Canada and the United States. He was ordained by the Canadian Presbyterian Church and dispatched as a missionary to Taiwan. At age 34, he began his work in a region that was largely unfamiliar to Westerners.
Medical Work
Macdonald established the first Western medicine clinic in northern Taiwan, providing free medical care to the local population. He treated patients from all social backgrounds, often traveling on foot or by horse to reach remote villages. His medical work was instrumental in gaining the trust of the local community and served as a gateway for his evangelistic efforts.
Educational Contributions
His educational legacy is perhaps his most enduring contribution:

偕醫學堂 (Ochong Medical School, 1880): Founded the first modern medical school in northern Taiwan, training local physicians in Western medicine. The school later became part of the National Taiwan University system.
Tamsui Theological College (1881): Established to train Taiwanese pastors and evangelists, ensuring the sustainability of the church. This institution evolved into the current STM Taiwan (聖約翰大學 / Taiwan Theological College and Seminary).
Girls’ Education: Macdonald was a pioneer in advocating for girls’ education in 19th-century Taiwan, establishing schools for girls at a time when this was highly unconventional.

Evangelism
Macdonald walked an estimated 87,500 kilometers across northern Taiwan during his 29-year mission. He:

Established over 60 churches across northern Taiwan
Baptized more than 1,700 converts
Trained and ordained numerous Taiwanese pastors who continued his work after his death
Used the local language (Hokkien) in his preaching, learning it within months of arrival

Language and Cultural Work
Macdonald developed a romanization system for the Hokkien language (known as the “Macdonald system” or 馬唐字) to facilitate Bible translation and local preaching. He also wrote a Hokkien dictionary and grammar, contributing to linguistic scholarship.
Death and Legacy
馬偕博士 died on June 2, 1901, in Tamsui, Taiwan, from a leg infection that he contracted while visiting a patient in a remote area. Despite his deteriorating health, he continued his work until his final days. He was buried in the church cemetery in Tamsui, where his grave remains a historical site.
His death deeply affected the Taiwanese Christian community. According to historical accounts, thousands of Taiwanese people — both Christian and non-Christian — mourned his passing, testifying to the depth of his impact on the region.
Institutions Carrying His Legacy

偕醫中學 (Ochong Teachers College): Now part of the National Taiwan University system
STM Taiwan (台灣神學院): Direct descendant of the Tamsui Theological College he founded
馬偕紀念醫院 (Mackay Memorial Hospital): One of Taiwan’s largest hospital networks, named in his honor
馬偕紀念醫院宜蘭分院: Branch hospital continuing his medical mission
真理大學 (Tunghais University): Has connections to his educational legacy

Commemoration
馬偕博士’s 150th anniversary of missionary work in Taiwan was commemorated in 2022, including special worship services such as the 馬偕博士台灣宣教150週年紀念主日 hosted by Good Shepherd Taiwanese Presbyterian Church on March 6, 2022.
His legacy continues through the many institutions he founded, including STM Taiwan (where Rev. Ming Yuan Hsu studied), the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan, and Mackay Memorial Hospital.

people/guo-yingyan.content:
Guo Yingyan (郭應言)
Guo Yingyan (郭應言, Rev. Guo / 郭牧師) was a pastor connected with the early development of Irvine Taiwanese Presbyterian Church (爾灣台灣基督長老教會 (PCT)). The church’s official history identifies him as a pastor who served ITPC after the departure of the founding-stage pastor 鄭泉聲牧師.
ITPC Role
The ITPC history document states that after 鄭泉聲牧師 returned to Japan, the congregation invited nearby pastors to help with pastoral care until 郭應言牧師 was called approximately a year later. It describes 郭應言牧師 as previously serving at a “House of Christ” church context and notes that he resigned after about one year because he was not accustomed to the Presbyterian church system.
Historical Significance
郭應言牧師’s brief service reflects the transitional period between ITPC’s founding independence and its later full-time pastoral stability. His tenure sits in the late-1990s period when the congregation was still worshiping at Creekside Fellowship Church and seeking durable pastoral leadership.
Source Notes and Confidence

Rev. Jonah Chang (張瑞雄)
Rev. Jonah Chang (張瑞雄) was a former minister of the Presbyterian Church of Formosa who, while serving the United Methodist Church in Fresno, California, led the one-month experimental Formosan church in Los Angeles in August 1970 that catalyzed the permanent Formosan Christian Church / FPCLA.

Role in FPCLA Origins
August 1970 Experimental Church
From Dr. Albert S. Lai’s 1971 dissertation:

In August 1970, Rev. Jonah Chang started a one-month experimental church to test feasibility of a Formosan congregation in Los Angeles.
First experimental Sunday worship: August 9, 1970 — 22 adults and 11 children attended.
After four Sundays, when Chang returned to Fresno at month’s end, the majority decided to organize a permanent church without a settled pastor and without outside financial support.
Early facility support came via Centenary United Methodist Church and Rev. Peter Chen (Wesley Hall) until the move to Wilshire Crest Presbyterian Church in July 1971.

Pastor Pingtung Lai (賴炳烔, Lai Ping-tung) was a Taiwanese Presbyterian pastor, Bible Society pioneer, and evangelist. He was a student of Dr. Barclay at Tainan Theological College and Seminary (TTCS), built Beigang Church, founded United Bible Societies work in Taiwan, and established Good Friend Mission. His son, Dr. Albert S. Lai (賴信雄), documented this heritage in the Self-Preface material tied to Toward A Community of Hope (1971 / 2025 reprint).

Core roles: Presbyterian pastor; Bible Society founder; evangelist; Good Friend Mission pioneer

Life & Ministry (three stages)

Pastoral ministry — Huwei, Chingliao, Ailan (Wu-niu-lan), Beigang (built church); Centennial Doubling Campaign evangelistic officer; assisted US church planting
Bible missions — founded United Bible Societies work in Taiwan from Beigang, then Taichung office/warehouse; translation/distribution; advisory network including KMT-era Christian officials (e.g. 張群, 周聯華, 馬壽華)

people/tahs-member-onboarding.title: TAHS member onboarding
people/tahs-member-onboarding.content:
TAHS Member Onboarding
TAHS Member Onboarding is the lightweight induction pathway for people who are being introduced into the Taiwanese American Historical Society (台美人歷史學會 (TAHS)) and the Echopedia historical-record workflow.
This page exists to give public wiki links a stable destination. It does not publish private rosters, internal spreadsheets, personal contact details, or administrative credentials.
Public-Facing Purpose
TAHS onboarding should help a new member understand:

the mission of preserving Taiwanese American historical memory;
the role of Echopedia as a living community archive;
how identity, names, titles, and contribution records are documented carefully;
privacy expectations for personal information, family records, photos, and testimony;
how to contribute corrections, memories, documents, and source leads.

Basic Onboarding Flow

Introduction — a current TAHS/Echopedia contact introduces the person and their historical or volunteer context.
Identity confirmation — names are recorded with Chinese characters, romanized forms, and role context where available.
Consent boundary — the person should understand what can be public, what should remain private, and what needs explicit permission before publication.
Role or title note — if a formal TAHS role is assigned, record the title and scope in the appropriate society or person page only after confirmation.
Contribution path — direct the person to the community contribution hub for memories, photos, documents, corrections, and source leads.
Review loop — published records remain correctable; community members may submit updates as new evidence appears.

Privacy and Safety Rules

Do not publish private phone numbers, private email addresses, home addresses, private spreadsheets, or internal administration links.
Treat family history, immigration stories, political history, church records, and elder testimony with consent-aware care.
Prefer public source links, official documents, and contributor-approved material.
If a person asks for a correction or removal of sensitive information, route it through the Echopedia correction process.

people/yunching-yeh-davis.content:
Dr. Yunching Yeh Davis (葉芸青)
Dr. Yunching Yeh Davis (葉芸青) served as Moderator of the National Taiwanese Presbyterian Council (NTPC) of the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) and authored the NTPC foreword “Half a Century of Faith and Mission” for the 2025 republication of Dr. Albert S. Lai’s 1971 dissertation Toward A Community of Hope.
Identity Snapshot

English: Dr. Yunching Yeh Davis
Chinese: 葉芸青
Era: Contemporary (NTPC Moderator at 2025 republication)
Geography: United States (NTPC / Taiwanese American Presbyterian network)
Core roles: NTPC Moderator; historical-ministry advocate; foreword author

Role in the 2025 Republication

Primary work page: Toward A Community of Hope (work & sources)
Full text (GitHub): complete extract

In the NTPC foreword, Dr. Yeh Davis framed Lai’s work as both theological and prophetic: at a time when Taiwanese immigrant churches in North America were still in their infancy—especially FPCLA, the first of its kind on the continent—Lai called the church to become a missional community, not merely a haven for immigrants.
Key themes:

Spiritual call amid cultural transition
From ethnic church to missional community — FPCLA as a “mission base”
Hopeful community theology
Unfinished mission across generations
